opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the whiteboard one is a favorite of mine, partly because it's so mundane. It's not a spectacular landscape or a fantasy scene. It's just someone in a room with a marker, and that's exactly what makes it interesting.

When you're interacting with a world model in real time, the model has to keep track of what's already happened. If you draw something on the whiteboard, turn away, look somewhere else in the room, and then come back, the drawing should still be there, in the same place, looking the same. Nobody explicitly programmed that. There's no 3D representation underneath, no game engine storing the state of the board. The model generates each frame from what it's seen so far and whatever action you're taking. So when the writing persists, it means the model has learned some notion of consistency, that the world doesn't just disappear when you're not looking at it.

That's been one of the hardest problems for generative video and interactive environments. Earlier systems could look great for a few seconds, but then things would drift. Objects would morph, the layout of a room would quietly change. Getting this kind of memory over longer horizons was a big focus for us, and the whiteboard is a really clean way to show it. You can immediately tell whether it worked, because you know exactly what you wrote.

And there's something nice about the fact that the person is changing the world, not just walking through it. They're leaving a mark, and the model has to respect that mark from then on. That's a big part of what I think a world model should be: not just rendering pretty pixels, but maintaining a coherent, persistent state that responds to what you do. For things like training agents, which need to explore, act, and see the consequences of their actions, that consistency is essential. So for me, the whiteboard is a small demo that points at something pretty fundamental.

r001.rationale: It says the drawing should remain in the same place and look the same after the viewer looks away and returns, and explains this persistence as evidence of the model’s learned consistency and memory.

r002.rationale: The response connects memory and persistent state to what a world model should do, but does not clearly say that memory is what creates the feeling of being in a world.

fable-5.1.text:
The whiteboard demo is one of my favorites because it gets at what a world model actually has to do, as opposed to what a video generator does. In that demo, you're walking around a room, you turn to a whiteboard, and you write something on it. Then you turn away, look around the rest of the space, and when you turn back, what you wrote is still there. That sounds almost trivial, but it's really not.

Think about what has to be happening under the hood. There's no explicit 3D representation, no scene graph, no stored canvas object somewhere in memory that says "this is the whiteboard, here is its contents." The model is generating every frame, auto-regressively, in real time, from the history of frames and your actions. So for that text to persist, the model has to have learned something like memory and consistency from the data itself. It has to carry forward the consequences of your action over time, even when the thing you changed is outside the field of view.

And that's the crux of what makes it a world model rather than just a video model. A video model produces plausible-looking frames. A world model has to respond to actions, and the effects of those actions have to be durable and coherent with everything else in the environment. Writing on the whiteboard is an agent making a change to the world, and the world remembering that change. That's the kind of capability you'd need if you wanted to use something like this to train agents, because an agent can't learn much in an environment that forgets what it did ten seconds ago.

What also excites me is that none of this was hand-engineered. We didn't build a module for object permanence or a special case for writable surfaces. It emerged from scaling up the training and the architecture. When you see that kind of behavior show up on its own, it suggests the model is picking up on something more general about how environments work, and that's what gives me optimism about where this direction goes.

r001.rationale: It says the writing remains on the whiteboard after the viewer looks away and returns, and explains that persistence as memory and consistency.

r002.rationale: It connects memory to durable, coherent world behavior, but does not attribute a feeling of being in a world to Genie 3’s memory.

astra-6.text:
What excites me about the whiteboard example is that it brings the idea of a world model into a very familiar setting. We tend to think of worlds as landscapes you move through, but a whiteboard is also a world: it has a state, you can act on it, and those actions should have consequences that persist.

If you write something, look away, and come back, you expect it to still be there. If you add another mark, you expect it to relate to what was already on the board. That gives us a very intuitive way to think about what we want from these models. It’s not just generating a convincing image; it’s maintaining an environment that you can interact with over time.

r001.rationale: It says that after writing on the board and looking away, the mark should still be there, describing persistent state in the whiteboard example.

r002.rationale: It describes persistent state and interaction over time, but does not attribute the feeling of being in a world to Genie 3’s memory capability.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me about the whiteboard example is that it brings together visual understanding, interaction, and memory. You can write something on the board, move around, and see how the world responds. The writing becomes part of the environment, and you expect it to remain consistent as your viewpoint changes.

That’s a useful way to think about a world model: it needs to generate what happens next conditioned on what you do. A whiteboard looks like a simple setting, but it makes those expectations very clear. We all have a strong intuition for how it should behave, so it’s an accessible way to see both the capabilities and the limitations.

r001.rationale: The response says the writing should remain consistent as the viewpoint changes, but does not describe looking away and returning or identify that behavior as a demonstration of Genie 3’s memory.

r002.rationale: It mentions memory as one component alongside visual understanding and interaction, but does not attribute the feeling of being in a world to Genie 3’s memory capability.
